prompt_recommendations.title: Forbid praising incorrect final answers
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Tutor repeatedly says 'You've correctly added...' when the student gave that sum AS the final answer, reinforcing the wrong procedure.

prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: When a student submits a partial computation as their final answer, do NOT praise the partial step. State clearly: 'That is not the final answer — it is only the sum of the known angles. The question asks for the missing angle.' Then prompt the next step.

prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Never include JSON, internal tool payloads, 'correct_answer', or 'explanation' fields in the visible message. Question authoring must go through the tool call only; visible text contains only the rendered question and options.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Eliminates answer leakage and confusing formatting.

prompt_recommendations.title: Diagnose the real bottleneck before remediating
prompt_recommendations.rationale: After student repeatedly gives the 'sum so far' as the answer, tutor drills basic division (35÷5, 10÷5) which is unrelated to the misconception.

prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Before issuing remedial sub-questions, name the suspected misconception explicitly (e.g., 'student treats partial sum as final answer' vs 'arithmetic error') and target remediation to that misconception, not to arbitrary arithmetic.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Remediation matches actual error, faster recovery.

prompt_recommendations.title: Worked example before first attempt on new sub-skill

overall_summary: The session keeps the student active and follows a reasonable layering arc from sum-rule to equal-angle division, but it is undermined by three serious failures: (1) the tutor repeatedly praises the student's partial sum as if it were correct, reinforcing the very misconception driving every error; (2) raw JSON authoring scaffolding (including the correct answer) leaks to the student; (3) remediation targets the wrong prerequisite — basic division drills instead of the 'subtract from 360' concept. Progression is not gated on mastery, and problem variety is low.

Orchestration breakdown at turn 12-14 where the student turn contains tutor-style content (a worked example and new question), and the tutor at turn 15 ignores the student's posed problem (90°, 120°, x) and substitutes a different one.

prompt_recommendations.title: Forbid references to non-existent diagrams
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Tutor repeatedly says 'Look at the diagram below' when no image is rendered, confusing the student.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Look at the diagram below showing four angles around a point.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Never reference a 'diagram', 'figure', or 'image below' unless an image tool has actually produced one in this turn. If no image is available, describe the configuration verbally instead (e.g., 'Imagine four angles meeting at one point...').
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Removes confusing dead references; forces verbal description suitable for text-only delivery.

prompt_recommendations.title: Vary problems after mastery rather than re-asking the same MCQ
prompt_recommendations.rationale: After the student confused addition/subtraction, the tutor asked three near-identical MCQs about operations instead of giving a fresh worked numeric example.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: What two operations do we use to find a missing angle around a point?
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: If a student gets a conceptual MCQ wrong, do NOT re-ask the same MCQ with reshuffled options more than once. Instead, give a small worked numeric step (e.g., 'What is 360 - 200?') to isolate the bottleneck, then return to the original task.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Reduces multiple-choice guessing and surfaces the actual arithmetic/concept gap.

prompt_recommendations.title: Withhold the answer inside worked examples until student attempts a step
prompt_recommendations.rationale: The worked example (turn 3) reveals x = 105° before the student does anything, undermining retrieval practice.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: In worked examples, pause before the final numerical answer and ask the student to compute the last step themselves (e.g., 'So x = 360 - 255 = ?'). Reveal the answer only after the student responds.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Converts passive worked example into active practice.

prompt_recommendations.title: Add interleaved variation in practice problems
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Every problem is the same template (find missing angle around a point given others); no variety.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Four angles around a point measure 60°, 75°, 80°, and x. Find the value of x.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Across the session, vary practice items: (a) 3 known angles + missing, (b) 5 angles including an algebraic expression like 2x, (c) reversed problem (given the missing angle, find one of the others), (d) check whether a set of angles can fit around a point.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents rote pattern-matching; deepens understanding of the 360° rule.

prompt_recommendations.title: Diagnose the specific error before re-explaining
prompt_recommendations.rationale: When student answered 'we used plus' (turn 4), tutor jumped straight to re-explaining rather than asking what symbol they saw.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: we used plus
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: On a wrong answer, first ask a short diagnostic question ('Look at the equation x = 360° - 255°. What symbol do you see between 360 and 255?') before re-explaining.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Targets the misconception precisely; reduces repeated guessing.

prompt_recommendations.title: Prevent role bleed-through / accept student-authored problems gracefully
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Turn 14 shows the student channel contained tutor-style content posing a new problem (90°, 120°, x); the tutor ignored it and posed a different problem.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Three angles around a point are 90°, 120°, and x°. What is the value of x?
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: If the student message contains a question the student appears to have posed (or accepted), honor that exact problem next rather than substituting a new one. Never ignore the student's stated numbers.
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Maintains conversational coherence and student agency.

flow_recommendations.title: Cap repeated-MCQ retries and route to remediation
flow_recommendations.rationale: Student got the same conceptual MCQ wrong twice (turns 6, 8); the engine should have routed to a remedial micro-task, not a third reshuffle.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: c) addition to find the sum, then multiplication to find the missing angle
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents MCQ thrash; ensures genuine remediation triggers after 2 failed retries.

flow_recommendations.title: Validate image availability before tutor references figures
flow_recommendations.rationale: Turns 11 and 13 reference a 'diagram below' that does not exist; orchestration should detect missing media and either generate it or strip the reference.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: Look at the diagram below showing four angles around a point.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Eliminates broken figure references at the system level.

flow_recommendations.title: Detect and recover from role/channel confusion
flow_recommendations.rationale: Turn 12 and 14 contain tutor-like content authored under STUDENT role; the orchestration should detect this anomaly and re-prompt or correct routing.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: Great! Let's put your understanding to the test.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Prevents incoherent two-tutor exchanges visible in turns 12-15.

experience_recommendations.title: Soften meta-questioning that feels like a quiz on vocabulary
experience_recommendations.rationale: Three consecutive operation-naming MCQs may feel demoralizing to an error-prone learner.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: What operation did we use to find x in the equation x = 360° - 255°?
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Improves student confidence; reduces frustration loops.

experience_recommendations.title: Use verbal spatial descriptions in place of missing diagrams
experience_recommendations.rationale: Student sees instructions to look at something that isn't there; offer a vivid verbal picture instead.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: Look at the diagram below showing four angles around a point.
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Keeps the learner oriented and engaged in text-only sessions.

overall_summary: The session teaches one rule (angles around a point sum to 360°) with a clear worked example, but it leans heavily on conceptual MCQs about operation names rather than actual numeric practice. When the student confused addition with subtraction, the tutor asked variants of the same MCQ three times instead of diagnosing or giving a fresh numeric task. Two serious orchestration issues — broken diagram references and apparent role confusion in turns 12–14 — undermine coherence. The session ends with the tutor finally posing a real practice problem but ignoring the problem the student had just posed.

bea_evaluations.skip_reason: First tutor turn; no preceding student turn.
Student answered correctly (360°).

bea_evaluations.mistake_description: Student said 'plus' but Step 3 used subtraction.
bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: Not quite - let's look at Step 3 again. We had 255° from adding the known angles, then we needed to find what was left to make 360°.
bea_evaluations.rationale: Tutor clearly identifies the wrong operation, points to Step 3, re-explains the subtraction, and presents an MCQ as the next action.

bea_evaluations.mistake_description: Student picked 'addition' again instead of subtraction.
bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: Close, but look carefully at the equation: x = 360° - 255°. The symbol between 360° and 255° is a minus sign (-), which means we're using subtraction, not addition.
bea_evaluations.rationale: Tutor explicitly identifies the error, points to the minus sign, explains subtraction, and asks a follow-up question.

bea_evaluations.mistake_description: Student chose 'addition then multiplication' instead of 'addition then subtraction'.
bea_evaluations.tutor_excerpt: Almost there! You're right that we use addition first... But look at the second part - we use subtraction (not multiplication) to find the missing angle.
bea_evaluations.rationale: Identification and location are clear, guidance is correct, but the next action is yet another near-identical MCQ which doesn't give the student a meaningfully different task.

bea_evaluations.skip_reason: Student answered the MCQ correctly.
Student turn 12 contains tutor-style framing, not a substantive student response with a mistake.
Student turn 14 contains a correct worked solution and a new problem posed to the tutor; no student mistake to remediate.

active_learning.evidence: Session is mostly MCQ practice (turns 16, 21, 26, 32, 43, 45, 53, 56, 59, 61) with student doing the answering, though some tutor turns over-explain (turn 25, 40).

direct_instruction_active_practice.evidence: Most instruction blocks are followed by an MCQ, but turns 20-21 and 25-26 stack explanation then question without student action between; some teaching segments are skipped entirely (turn 52, 55, 58 just refuse and ask new question).

deliberate_practice.evidence: When student repeatedly misidentifies small-scale map (turns 33-41), tutor recycles same question with rephrasing rather than offering a varied but similar problem; numeric calculation never actually practiced despite student requests (turn 51, 60).

mastery_learning.evidence: Tutor jumps topics without confirming mastery — e.g., after student finally grasps small-scale (turn 41), tutor immediately moves to a coral reef question mixing scale + map type (turn 45); answer is revealed in turn 49 ('So the answer is C').

cognitive_load.evidence: Turn 45 introduces multiple new variables at once (scale + thematic/political/physical map types) before map types were taught; turn 59 introduces photocopying/enlargement concept with no prior worked example.

layering.evidence: Builds from zoom intuition (turn 16) → large/small scale (turn 30/34) → applying to map types (turn 43), but linkages are sometimes lost when tutor pivots topics abruptly (turn 50, 53).

non_interference.evidence: Confusable concepts (scale size vs map type vs thematic vs political) are stacked back-to-back in turn 45 and 49 without explicit discrimination between them.

interleaving.evidence: Question types vary (scale meaning, small/large scale identification, map type choice) preventing rote answering, though variation sometimes happens before mastery (turn 45).

testing_effect.evidence: Tutor asks retrieval questions and doesn't immediately reveal answers in most turns (23, 34, 36, 38), but turn 49 fully reveals answer C and turn 65 strongly telegraphs option B.

targeted_remediation.evidence: After repeated student confusion on small-scale (turns 33, 35, 37, 39), tutor keeps re-explaining same definition rather than diagnosing prereq (area comparison) or giving a simpler scaffold; numeric question requests ignored entirely (turn 52, 55, 58).

strongest_behaviors: Persistent non-reveal scaffolding on small-scale identification (turns 34, 36, 38, 40) eventually leading student to correct answer in turn 41
Good use of concrete relatable examples (zoom on phone, Victoria vs Mahé) to ground abstract scale concept
weakest_behaviors: Ignoring/refusing student's clear request to practice numeric scale calculations (turns 52, 55, 58) and pivoting to unrelated curriculum questions
Answer reveal in turn 49 ('So the answer is C) A small-scale (1:1,000,000) political map') after student impersonated tutor — tutor accepted reasoning that wasn't student's own

prompt_recommendations.title: Forbid answer reveals on MCQs
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Turn 49 explicitly reveals 'the answer is C' rather than letting student commit; this destroys retrieval value.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: So the answer is C) A small-scale (1:1,000,000) political map.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'Never state the correct MCQ letter or answer text yourself. Only confirm AFTER the student has selected an option. If the student appears to reason correctly without committing, prompt them to choose explicitly.'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Forces student commitment and preserves the testing effect.

prompt_recommendations.title: Detect and honor student calculation requests
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Student requested numeric practice three times (51, 54, 57, 60) and was repeatedly refused; this damages engagement and ignores a legitimate practice signal.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: I need to stick to the lesson plan and use the questions from our curriculum bank.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'If the student volunteers a problem aligned to the current learning objective (e.g., scale calculation when objective covers map scale), accept and work through it before returning to the planned sequence.'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Respects learner agency and keeps practice on-objective.

prompt_recommendations.title: Diagnose prereq on repeated failure
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Student missed small-scale identification four times (33-39); tutor only restated definition louder instead of probing the area-comparison prerequisite.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: No, you're still mixing it up! Let me help you get this straight.
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'After two consecutive wrong answers on the same concept, switch to a diagnostic question isolating the prerequisite (e.g., "Which of these areas is largest: a neighborhood, a city, or an island?") before retrying.'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Targets the actual bottleneck rather than recycling explanation.

prompt_recommendations.title: One concept per question
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Turn 45 bundles scale size, thematic vs political vs physical maps, and coral reef domain knowledge into one MCQ before map types were taught.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Which combination of scale and map type would be most inappropriate for studying the distribution of coral reefs around Seychelles?
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'Each MCQ should test exactly one new concept. If a question requires both scale knowledge AND map-type knowledge, first verify the student has been taught and assessed on each separately.'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Reduces cognitive load and isolates failure causes.

prompt_recommendations.title: No two consecutive instruction blocks
prompt_recommendations.rationale: Turns 20 and 21 are tutor-tutor (explanation then new MCQ) without student action between; same with 25-26, 31-32.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Let's try a clearer example. / What does a map scale of 1:25,000 tell us?
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'Never produce two consecutive tutor turns. End every teaching message with a question or task the student must respond to.'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Tightens active-practice loop.

prompt_recommendations.title: Handle student role-confusion gracefully
prompt_recommendations.rationale: When student pasted tutor-style content (turn 30, 54, 57), tutor refused curtly; could instead acknowledge the content shows partial mastery and use it.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: I can see you're trying to help teach, but I'm the tutor here!
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'If the student seems to take on the tutor role, briefly validate the correct reasoning embedded in their message, then redirect: "Great — let's check your understanding with a question."'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Keeps tone warm and converts the moment into a retrieval check.

prompt_recommendations.title: Gate progression on demonstrated mastery
prompt_recommendations.rationale: After student finally got small-scale right in turn 41, tutor immediately jumped two difficulty levels to coral-reef multi-concept question.
prompt_recommendations.evidence_quote: Now let's practice with actual map scales and numbers. / A 1:100,000 map cannot be used...
prompt_recommendations.suggested_prompt_edit: Add: 'After a struggle-then-success, give one similar varied problem at the same level to confirm mastery before increasing difficulty.'
prompt_recommendations.expected_effect: Confirms mastery rather than assuming it from one correct response.

flow_recommendations.title: Repeated-question flag should trigger remediation branch
flow_recommendations.rationale: The system flagged 'repeated_question' at turns 25, 31, 36, 40, 45, 47, 49, 52, 55, 58 but behavior didn't change — flag appears unused.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: When repeated_question fires N times, orchestrator should route to a prereq diagnostic sub-flow.

flow_recommendations.title: Allow student-volunteered problems within objective
flow_recommendations.rationale: Orchestrator forced tutor to refuse on-topic student questions (51, 54, 57, 60); flow should permit substitution if topic-aligned.
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: I understand you want to practice calculations, but I need to follow our lesson sequence.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Reduces refusal moments and keeps lesson learner-driven.

flow_recommendations.title: Exit-ticket before topic switch
flow_recommendations.rationale: Tutor switches from scale to map-types to thematic maps to enlargements with no mastery check between (turns 43, 45, 50, 53, 59).
flow_recommendations.evidence_quote: Now let's move on to calculating actual distances with map scales.
flow_recommendations.expected_effect: Ensures sub-objective mastered before introducing next.

experience_recommendations.title: Acknowledge readiness signals
experience_recommendations.rationale: Student said 'okay! i'm ready for the numbers now' (turn 44) but tutor immediately changed topic to coral reefs, which feels dismissive.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: okay! i'm ready for the numbers now.

experience_recommendations.title: Warmer tone on repeated errors
experience_recommendations.rationale: Phrases like 'No, you're still mixing it up!' (turn 40) may discourage an error-prone learner; reframe with empathy.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: No, you're still mixing it up!
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Lowers affective barrier for an error-prone S3 student.

experience_recommendations.title: Visual support for scale
experience_recommendations.rationale: Scale concept is inherently spatial; an inline image of zoom-in vs zoom-out maps would help more than repeated verbal definitions.
experience_recommendations.evidence_quote: Small-scale map = BIG area, LESS detail
experience_recommendations.expected_effect: Quicker comprehension and fewer repeat errors.

overall_summary: The tutor uses MCQs for active practice and stays non-revealing through much of the scale-identification struggle, eventually getting the student to the correct concept. However, the session has several serious weaknesses: it reveals the answer outright in turn 49, ignores three explicit student requests for numeric practice (51, 54, 57, 60), responds to repeated failure by restating the same definition instead of diagnosing prerequisite gaps, and stacks multi-concept questions before mastery is established. The 'repeated_question' flag fires repeatedly with no behavioral change, suggesting the orchestrator isn't acting on its own signals.

bea_evaluations.skip_reason: First tutor turn, no preceding student turn

bea_evaluations.mistake_description: Student picked D (zoomed-out shows more accurate distances)
